paragraphs: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, follow Terrence O’Brien. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

On October 29th, The New York Times reported that Nvidia co-founder and showman CEO Jensen Huang appeared to be the target of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, previously told The Verge. “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.”

The Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps as early as 2024. Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities confiscated her passport back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing.

This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions. Meanwhile, he had gotten quite cozy with President Trump, once even putting him on speakerphone on-stage at the All-In Summit.
Then last week, things escalated quickly.

On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO, though there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature.

On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was launching an investigation into its CEO shortly after.

Many believed that Jensen Huang would survive the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review, 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015, which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider.)

Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening. According to Bloomberg, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.”
On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia.

CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “extraordinarily difficult period.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.”

But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th. It closed at $162.85 on November 13th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China, and the industry in general. The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure.

Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “completely normal and not unusual.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “national security concerns” without naming anyone specifically. According to Reuters, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang.

Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “bring back THE boss,” on an internal post.

Some even speculated that Jensen Huang was the victim of a vast conspiracy, whether that was a coup by some faction within Nvidia, or perhaps the goal of China all along had simply been to chase him from the CEO chair.
By Thursday night, Reuters reported a third affair, this one also with an Nvidia employee, though no further information has emerged.

First and foremost for Nvidia, it must find a new CEO. It’s possible that Kress eventually ceases to be “interim” CEO, but other names, including Apple’s hardware chief Johny Srouji, have also been rumored. (Donald Trump believes they should hire Tim Cook, but to call that unlikely would be an understatement.)

It’s also possible that Nvidia will undergo a dramatic reorganization. Whoever takes over as CEO is unlikely to keep the 60 direct reports of Jensen Huang. With a first-ever board chair in Jones, it’s also possible that the board of directors will play a larger role in the company going forward.

The board’s investigation into Jensen Huang that began on November 8th is ongoing. The scandal is likely to drag on for some time. With the possibility that Jensen Huang will have to testify before Congress, the company may choose to be proactive about disclosing any additional information publicly.

The incoming Democratic majority is expected to come down harder on Silicon Valley than the current Republican Congress. While it’s unclear just how far the new House and Senate will go in trying to rein in the tech industry and its billionaire leaders, it’s possible it will try to make an example of Nvidia as an early act of strength. If Nvidia is found to have been turning a blind eye to companies like Megaspeed, which are suspected of funneling advanced chips to China, it could face civil or criminal penalties. And it seems increasingly likely that stricter trade restrictions will be implemented on Nvidia’s chips, which could increase tensions with China in an already costly trade war.

There is a possibility that Jensen Huang could face criminal charges. In May, he claimed that Nvidia had “zero percent” market share in China due to stringent export restrictions. But shortly after, Culper Research published a report claiming that in reality over 20 percent of the company’s 2026 compute revenue was from China, though that number has not been independently verified. The report cited “illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries” as the primary source of those revenues. Among the largest of those intermediaries, according to Culper Research, was Megaspeed, which Nvidia repeatedly vouched for to the US government.

If proof is established that the CEO was knowingly helping Megaspeed or any other companies to illegally divert restricted chips to China, he could face criminal charges. And, as The Verge’s Elizabeth Lopatto put it, “under a functioning legal system, [he] could actually go to jail.”
There is the chance that members of the current administration are also tied up in this scandal, as it’s unclear how much the White House knew and when.

Considering Nvidia’s sizable investments, borrowing to build data centers, and the importance of its hardware, there are tons of open questions about how this impacts not just the AI industry, but the American economy as a whole. Nvidia is essentially propping up a large part of the tech industry and, if money stops flowing out of its coffers, it could drag a lot of other companies down with it.

There are also open questions about how this impacts the American public’s perception of the AI industry. The new Democratic majority was elected in part by campaigning against AI companies and the explosion of data center buildout across the country. That one of its more prominent CEOs is now embroiled in a spying scandal and multiple extramarital affairs probably isn’t going to endear the industry to the public.
Megaspeed was the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia, but when Singaporean newspaper The Straits Times visited its office in October of 2025, it found “no signs of activity.”

Megaspeed is just one of multiple companies that Nvidia has been approved to sell chips with suspicious offices. The New York Times described New Matrix’s headquarters as “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.”

Jensen Huang’s connections to Super Micro are also under scrutiny. Earlier this year, one of its founders, an employee, and a contractor for the company were indicted by the Justice Department for conspiring to violate American export controls and divert Nvidia chips to China.

While a lot has changed, it’s still worth reading the Times’ first big report from October 29th that lays the groundwork for the eventual deluge of international intrigue and infidelity that ultimately led to Jensen Huang’s downfall.
The New York Times paints a fascinating portrait of Alice Huang who now finds herself at the center of an international espionage scandal.
The Decoder interview with Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, digs into what China hoped to get out of Jensen Huang.

The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions. Then last week, things escalated quickly.

On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO, though there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature.

Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “bring back THE boss,” on an internal post.

Some even speculated that Jensen Huang was the victim of a vast conspiracy, whether that was a coup by some faction within Nvidia, or perhaps the goal of China all along had simply been to chase him from the CEO chair.

https://www.theverge.com/streaming/10356.title: YouTube found a new way to inflate view counts
https://www.theverge.com/streaming/10356.author: Emma Roth
paragraphs: YouTube’s view counts will now include the number of people that it estimates are watching a video together on TV. In an update on Monday, the platform says it’s bringing “co-views” to public view counts across long-form videos, Shorts, and live content to provide a more “complete picture” of how people are using its platform.

YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also says the change will help it align with “TV industry standards,” which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching shows. The company says it doesn’t use devices, like cameras or microphones, to estimate how many people are watching a video on TV. Instead, it estimates co-views using a “privacy safe statistical model” that takes into account “demographic patterns and viewing times.”

This marks yet another update to YouTube’s view count system. In August, the platform began counting a view as soon as a video starts playing. The company said at the time that creators will notice their view counts increasing faster as a result of this change, and it seems like adding co-views could boost these numbers as well.

YouTube notes that it will only apply co-views to new views on TV going forward, and that they won’t appear retroactively. Co-views also won’t affect a creator’s ad revenue, YouTube Partner Program eligibility, or revenue.

https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/1.title: ‘It’s a risk’: How Rockstar built the most detailed (and romantic) GTA yet
https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/1.author: Andrew Webster
paragraphs: Grand Theft Auto VI isn’t just the biggest GTA game to date; it’s also the most romantic. Though the series is well known for its sordid assortment of criminal leads, GTA VI switches things up by starring a pair of thieves who also happen to fall in love after meeting while stealing a car. It’s still an open-world action game full of chaos and mayhem. But many players will also be attempting to nurture the budding relationship in between heists. The sprawling game is designed to support both audiences.

“It’s a risk,” explains Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North. “It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”

Despite the couple — named Jason and Lucia — being so central to the GTA VI experience, the development of the game didn’t start with characters or story. It began with a place. Nelson says that “pretty quickly” the team settled on placing the game in Leonida, the GTA universe’s version of Florida and the setting of one of the series’ most iconic games, Vice City on the PS2. In 2015, a small group of developers from Rockstar headed to Florida to get a sense of the place and set the groundwork for what would go on to become GTA VI.

“We just went around to feel it out,” explains Nelson. “Go to the Everglades, go to the Keys, go to the city, as many places as we can, and start thinking about what aspects of the place we want to incorporate. And then the map team starts building our version of that and talking very loosely and very broadly about what types of people we want to include and what types of places.”

The team realized they wanted to tell a story that would pull players through the various locations they were creating. And the best way to do that was to have characters who were relatively small-time criminals. They would start near the bottom of the criminal underworld and work their way up, traversing Leonida’s various locations, culminating in the splashy Vice City.

At the same time, the developers also wanted to do something different with the character-switching mechanic from GTA V, which let players swap between three unique criminals, each with very different stories and motivations. For GTA VI, a couple working together to steal enough money to escape the outlaw life fit both of these ideas perfectly. But it also presented some new challenges.

“Could we make a relationship work?” Nelson remembers thinking. “It’d be very different from three characters living separate lives that come together for narrative purposes and then split. These two are going to need to be together all the time and that’s going to be a challenge. It felt really wrong to have these people that are supposedly together only be together when we’re giving you scripted content.”

While GTA V is the obvious reference point, the new GTA also builds off of Rockstar’s 2018 Western Red Dead Redemption 2. That game was notable in particular for giving players more ways to interact with the world: You could talk to any NPC, sit around a campfire while drinking coffee or playing cards, or grow out your beard for a new look.

GTA VI expands this in ways that are designed to reinforce the relationship aspect of the experience. For instance, not only can you drink coffee, but you can also make a cup and hand it to your partner. The two can spend time together sitting on the couch watching TV, or go out to a club and dance. There’s even a button dedicated exclusively to making Jason and Lucia hold hands when they’re together.
“If it’s additive, and it makes you laugh, we include it.”

Nelson notes that when the team implemented the hand-holding feature, it was a revelatory moment for showing how the story and gameplay could connect. “When we got that mechanic in — and it’s not just a toggle, it’s an active thing that you have to commit to and hold — it was a really profound thing,” he says.

But it’s also a careful balancing act. While RDR2 was a widely praised game, it also received criticism for its slow pace, which was due in large part to all of the small mechanical details. https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.title: Suno now lets you make AI videos for your AI music
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.author: Jess Weatherbed
paragraphs: Suno has introduced image and video generation in its latest effort to expand beyond being an AI music platform. The new feature, called “Visuals,” allows users to turn Suno songs into AI-generated video clips that automatically lipsync to lyrics, or make images via prompt descriptions that can be used as thumbnails and album artwork.

Visuals is available on web, iOS, and Android. The exact layout differs across Suno’s desktop and mobile interfaces, but users will find a new Visuals tab under Create mode on each version. Web users can also access Visuals by selecting the three dot menu on a song in their library. From there, users can select which section of the track to use, up to a maximum of 15 seconds, and select a reference image to build the generated video clip.

There are three options available for the starting image reference: selecting one of the original character presets provided by Suno, uploading your own photo or artwork, or generating the image directly on Suno using descriptive prompts. The image generation capabilities also allow users to select specific aspect ratios, optimizing results for landscape or portrait modes and online platforms.

For video generation, users can select whether the reference image is used as the start or end frame, making it easier to edit the 15-second clips together. There’s a toggle to automatically lipsync vocals to the generated video, and tools for adjusting aspect ratio and clip length. Visuals also includes a dedicated video editing timeline for assembling clips into longer videos, and adding customizable song lyric text.

The H3 Move AI model is being used to power Visuals, based on H3 from MiniMax. Suno says the AI has been “optimized for our community including adding additional protections and safeguards,” which include a “suite of new text and visual filters” designed to block people from using or generating the likeness of specific artists, public figures, copyrighted works and IP. Visuals also uses its own “Visuals credits” to generate videos and images, which are distinct from the song credits used to make AI music, meaning Suno users will have additional expenses to pay in order to use this new feature.

The Visuals launch follows Suno introducing a Speech feature in October for generating spoken words and voiceovers. Adding video capabilities is another attempt to diversify the platform after Suno’s music generator attracted a number of high-profile lawsuits, though it seems some users would rather the company focus on improving those song-generating capabilities. In the YouTube video for the Visuals launch, one user says “FIX AUDIO BEFORE ADDING CRAP NOBODY ASKED FOR” — a sentiment that other commenters are echoing.

https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.title: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.author: Terrence O'Brien
paragraphs: New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”

Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”

Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

https://www.theverge.com/policy/1036749/.title: Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
https://www.theverge.com/policy/1036749/.author: Justine Calma
paragraphs: President Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler. As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song.

Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — saying “Trump out.” Others say “Reject Pax Silica,” the name for the US-led international initiative to secure chips and critical minerals used in the hardware fueling the AI boom.
"Peace and prosperity for whom?"

“Pax” comes from the Latin word for “peace, stability, and long-term prosperity,” the Pax Silica website proudly says. Yet the unspoken question — peace and prosperity for whom? — explains the whiplash between the Philippine government’s warm welcome of Trump and the public fury raging outside.

Trump says he wants to “win AI” — whatever that means. As such, the US needs data centers full of GPUs to do it. With Americans increasingly opposed to data centers and chip factories being built in their communities, the US is now recruiting less affluent nations to take up some of the slack. Lawmakers from both the US and the Philippines are promising a slice of the riches that advances in generative AI are supposed to create. And that’s supposed to be worth the land razed, homes destroyed, and natural resources lost in the name of technological progress. In the Philippines, that’s taking the shape of a proposed 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) hub for chip factories, processing plants for critical minerals, and data centers.

At least two dozen countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative, and Trump was expected to pressure more to join while in the Philippines for events related to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. With Pax Silica, the US aims to insulate itself from China’s dominance in manufacturing semiconductors and processing critical minerals needed to make those chips. Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen to meet with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.

Philippine and US officials are expected to sign a framework agreement by the end of the year for the jointly developed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone. The details are still murky and shrouded in NDAs. The Philippines’ Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) overseeing the plan expects an economic boom from minerals processing and chip manufacturing, with perhaps a data center or two on site. Meanwhile, human rights advocates who oppose the project warn that it will displace Indigenous residents, cutting them off from water resources on which they rely.
“How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood?”

“We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.

The Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.”

The agency says the project will be on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.
"There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here"

The BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he said, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf.

He did mention, however, that an American energy company was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

Bingcang said in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley.

At the first chip fabs in California, workers — many of them Filipino immigrants — donned “bunny suits” to assemble sensitive chips in environmentally controlled “clean rooms.” Little did they know that the gear they wore offered little protection against the harsh chemicals used in manufacturing, which also leaked out of storage tanks to contaminate soil and groundwater. When studies came out in the ’90s documenting disproportionately high rates of miscarriages among workers, companies pledged to phase out some of the chemicals linked to reproductive health risks. Around the same time, chip manufacturing started to move out of the US to Asia, where similar health problems stemming from the same chemicals cropped up even decades later.

Chipmakers say their fabs have gotten much safer over the years, in part because more work is automated. Even so, the BCDA estimates that the AI hub will create up to 190,000 direct jobs. The BCDA, White House, and Philippine’s Malacañang Palace did not immediately respond to questions from The Verge.

“I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Trump told President Marcos during his visit. Marcos’ parents are estimated to have stolen up to $30 billion from government coffers over decades of rule before a people power movement ousted the current president’s father from the same office in the 1980s. But public memory, it seems, can be short.

And skyrocketing demand for more powerful chips used for generative AI has raised fears among environmental and labor groups that history might repeat itself. Companies move fast and break things, leaving a toxic mess in their wake. And when Americans decide they’ve had enough in their own back yards, the industry sets up shop somewhere else where they think their customers aren’t paying attention and politicians are happy to look the other direction.

“How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood?”

“We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.

There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.

The Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.”

The agency says the project will be on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.

"There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here"

The BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he said, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf.

He did mention, however, that an American energy company was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

Bingcang said in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley.

At the first chip fabs in California, workers — many of them Filipino immigrants — donned “bunny suits” to assemble sensitive chips in environmentally controlled “clean rooms.” Little did they know that the gear they wore offered little protection against the harsh chemicals used in manufacturing, which also leaked out of storage tanks to contaminate soil and groundwater. When studies came out in the ’90s documenting disproportionately high rates of miscarriages among workers, companies pledged to phase out some of the chemicals linked to reproductive health risks. Around the same time, chip manufacturing started to move out of the US to Asia, where similar health problems stemming from the same chemicals cropped up even decades later.

Chipmakers say their fabs have gotten much safer over the years, in part because more work is automated. Even so, the BCDA estimates that the AI hub will create up to 190,000 direct jobs. The BCDA, White House, and Philippine’s Malacañang Palace did not immediately respond to questions from The Verge.

“I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Trump told President Marcos during his visit. Marcos’ parents are estimated to have stolen up to $30 billion from government coffers over decades of rule before a people power movement ousted the current president’s father from the same office in the 1980s. But public memory, it seems, can be short.

And skyrocketing demand for more powerful chips used for generative AI has raised fears among environmental and labor groups that history might repeat itself. Companies move fast and break things, leaving a toxic mess in their wake. And when Americans decide they’ve had enough in their own back yards, the industry sets up shop somewhere else where they think their customers aren’t paying attention and politicians are happy to look the other direction.

As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1035924/nv.title: Nvidia’s rise, visualized
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1035924/nv.author: Sean Hollister
paragraphs: If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.

It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?

But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful company that might tempt a new CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.

It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.

If you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but shows you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.

TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.

Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering company is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.

Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.
Maybe that’d make people feel differently about data centers?

But even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.

And make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the company’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she announced. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.

Nvidia isn’t the only company whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.

But while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.

In the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.
On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.

Asked how things might change under new management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-important firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.
“Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”

Nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress said Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.
In other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the plan.
Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

https://www.theverge.com/policy/1036935/.author: Lauren Feiner
paragraphs: With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass new protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block users from filing lawsuits.

On Tuesday, members of a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hosted a hearing calling for the end of forced arbitration for online harms. Their immediate target was Roblox, which they accused of evading legal complaints about children allegedly groomed on the platform by enforcing its own forced arbitration clause against users who agreed to the terms as minors, in some cases even under the age of 10. Separately, a few blocks away, Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Laurel Lee (R-FL) brought hotel heiress Paris Hilton to Capitol Hill to advocate for the Defiance Act, which would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators.

“The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), who chairs the Judiciary subcommittee, told reporters after the Roblox hearing. “The more I see these companies evade regulations, the more I think there is nothing as powerful as a jury.” Hawley introduced a new bill with ranking member Dick Durbin (D-IL) to render arbitration agreements unenforceable for disputes over alleged child sexual exploitation or “child cyber injury,” which could include “reputational harm, mental suffering,” or death.
“The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors”

Roblox has sought to enforce its arbitration clause in lawsuits it’s facing over allegations that users were groomed on the gaming platform as minors, despite the company’s claims of protections. Roblox is facing about 180 lawsuits in a consolidated case over its alleged role in failing to protect children. Under the arbitration process, the public would not get to see legal discovery like the kind that’s come to light under recent cases against Meta. Hawley called the jury system “corruption-proof” and “an incredibly big hammer.”

Roblox has denied that it’s trying to dodge accountability. “Safety has been central to Roblox since we launched. We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” Roblox’s global head of public policy Nicky Jackson Colaço said in a statement. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Congress has only a little more than three more weeks left in session before the end of the year, and a new Democratic majority will be sworn in come January. Republicans are expected to do their best to push through President Donald Trump’s nominees for judgeships and executive branch posts like FCC commissioner in the lame-duck session, as well as try to pass year-end bills like the National Defense Authorization Act, which often includes a range of other policy items. But some lawmakers are holding out hope that they can open up courthouses to new litigation over deepfake abuse and child predation.

Litigation has become one of the more successful ways for survivors of online harm to seek change. Congress has failed to pass many prominent child safety, privacy, and consumer protection bills, though it has begun to tackle the deepfake issue through the Take It Down Act. At the same time, attorneys general and individual plaintiffs have collected significant settlements and legal wins despite the broad scope of tech’s legal shield, Section 230. If bills like the Defiance Act or those seeking to end forced arbitration were to pass, tech companies and perpetrators of online harms could become vulnerable to a new wave of legal challenges.
“You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court”

In addition to Hawley and Durbin’s bill about forced arbitration, Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Katie Britt (R-AL), and Cory Booker (D-NJ) introduced a similar bill with a slightly different approach, including explicitly covering data privacy violations. At the Roblox hearing, Northwestern University law professor Myriam Gilles, an expert on forced arbitration, said she’s testified before Congress many times on this topic, but “never expected to come before this body to talk about its use against 9 year olds.” Passing either proposal, she said, would have a profound impact. “You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court.”

The Defiance Act would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators for damages, in an attempt to raise the cost of creating these kinds of images. Hilton visited Washington earlier this year to share how an intimate non-deepfake video of her at age 19 shared without her consent impacted her life, and she used her story to advocate for the Defiance Act. At Tuesday’s press conference, she said she would come back to Congress as many times as necessary for the bill to become law. “Some people might have thought that was the end of my fight,” Hilton said. “But when I make a promise to survivors, I keep it.”

Hilton said over 50 million people have been victimized by sexually explicit deepfakes. “For me personally, strangers have created over 100,000 AI-generated explicit images and videos portraying me in the most graphic and disturbing ways imaginable,” Hilton said. “If this can happen to someone with my resources and my platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone.”

Hilton’s comments were followed by Elliston Berry, an advocate who said a classmate made an explicit deepfake image of her friend group “from an innocent social media post” when she was 14, and distributed it throughout her school. “In a matter of seconds, my sense of security disappeared,” she said. “For me, the Defiance Act means recognition that victims deserve to be heard, that their experience matters, and that their right to seek justice should not depend on how quickly technology advances.”

https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.title: What is Nvidia without AI’s sugar daddy in charge?
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.author: Elizabeth Lopatto
paragraphs: If the glorious AI revolution rests entirely on the well-being of one man, AI is perhaps not as robust a technology as I had previously been led to believe. Nonetheless, chunks of Silicon Valley are now insisting he is indispensable. For instance, if Elon Musk is telling the truth, then Jensen Huang (the former CEO of Nvidia, a company with a market cap of about $3 trillion) has been making deals that were “a handshake with Jensen” with suppliers — “not a written contract,” Musk wrote.

Fascinating stuff to tell shareholders. But after listening to Nvidia’s first earnings call with its new CEO, Colette Kress, I do think something may have shifted. In her former role as CFO, Kress generally told Huang to stop spending so much money on financing its customers, because telling the CEO to stop spending so much goddamn money is the CFO’s job. Apparently he belittled her about this, but that’s the CEO–CFO relationship, baby! Anyway she’s the boss now, at least temporarily. I think it’s reasonable to assume that though Nvidia has for years been the AI industry’s sugar daddy, without Huang and his handshakes in the picture, it may be less liberal with its cash.
"Kress shot down the idea that Huang’s departure would lead to a brain drain within Nvidia"

Kress’ job was never going to be easy. Even without tantrums from the likes of Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Musk, both of whom seem to have a lot of free time for guys who are ostensibly running multibillion-dollar companies, having to steer a company after an event on the scale of Huang’s meltdown is a miserable task. But this woman also is now having to deal with a bunch of guys publicly insisting that Huang was the only reason Nvidia succeeded. It amused me on the call that she did the thing I often do when men decide they can bully me, which is to tap in another man who is theoretically or actually in charge of me — and so on the call, Nvidia board Chair Harvey C. Jones politely told these losers to get bent. The board does not intend to reinstate Huang, and the company won’t be taking questions about him.

On the call, Kress pointedly noted that Nvidia’s agreements with suppliers last through the end of the decade, so I suppose we must entertain the possibility that when it comes to the handshake deals, Musk is, once again, lying. This is an important thing, though — as SemiAnalysis noted in its bizarrely conspiratorial post on the situation, Nvidia is successful because it has choked off the supply chain.

Kress also shot down the idea that Huang’s departure would lead to a brain drain within Nvidia, or the kind of open internal revolt that got Sam Altman reinstated at OpenAI during “the blip” in 2023. She told investors that “our employees, we believe, are committed. They are committed to doing their life’s work at Nvidia.” Nvidia’s employees have “been working seamlessly on what they need to complete,” she added. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual.” I’m sure we’ll hear more about this in the coming days, but unlike with Altman, Huang resigned, and we all know why. And while some employees support reinstating Huang, I notice that there’s a real dearth of “we’ll quit with him” in those sentiments.

I don’t think this is going to shut the Branch Nvidians up, but I do think the board doesn’t have another choice here. Hilariously, we learned this weekend that Nvidia did not buy complete directors’ and officers’ insurance. While the individual executives’ and board members’ personal assets are shielded from lawsuits that stem from its executives’ behavior, the company is not. So if someone, or perhaps several someones, were to file a suit because of, say, Huang’s personal life and its damaging effects on the stock price, Nvidia itself is on the hook.
"The scandal isn’t mainly about the affairs, as much fun as we all have been having with them"

This is to say nothing of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s investigation — which, given how cliqued up Huang was with President Donald Trump, may be investigating on his behalf rather than investigating him — or the California attorney general going on Bloomberg TV to say that he was going to start kicking the tires on an investigation, or Huang and general counsel Tim Teter’s upcoming congressional testimony. The three actual lawyers left at the Department of Justice may be doing their own investigation, too. Elizabeth Warren seems mad. Marco Rubio’s name has been publicly attached in stories on the leaks, which makes me a little suspicious about who’s been doing the leaking.

A reminder: The scandal isn’t mainly about the affairs, as much fun as we all have been having with them. It is about Nvidia customers allegedly circumventing a ban on selling chips to China. The scandal is already big enough that US policy has been altered; the Department of Commerce informed us all on November 16th that there were new restrictions on selling chips to countries such as Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. Also, data centers around the world need licenses from the US to lease compute to companies headquartered in China.
“No one could tell them ‘no’ or put them in their place.”

You may be wondering how these restrictions will affect Nvidia’s sales. The company also addressed this, though somewhat obliquely: It raised its forecast, saying that revenue will grow by 75 percent next year. Still, given that Singapore alone was responsible for $104 billion of revenue in 2025, I am curious about the number; at the time, it was the second-biggest geographic area by revenue, dwarfed only by the US. I can’t tell you how much Singaporean sales matter to Nvidia now, because around the time that Singaporean sales reportedly started to represent half the company’s revenue, Nvidia switched its reporting methodology. The company had previously noted that “most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant.” Notably, Megaspeed had a Singapore address — and was the subject of a truncated Commerce Department investigation into whether its chips were being diverted to China. Fun stuff!

You know what else is fun? Jensen Huang’s children are still at the company, at least as far as anyone knows. His daughter Madison, described as Huang’s “chief of staff” by The New York Times, even helped direct Nvidia’s response to inquiries about Megaspeed, which have been mounting now for a year, the Financial Times reported. Her husband, Nico Caprez, “was promoted to a role that covered international deals with cloud computing clients in Asia” around the time those inquiries were getting started. “They had a lot of power and influence and were allowed to operate unchecked,” an anonymous source told the FT. “No one could tell them ‘no’ or put them in their place.”

His kids — one of them, Spencer, ran a bar before his role at Nvidia — likely haven’t endeared themselves to their colleagues, based on some of the reporting now trickling out about them. What was Spencer doing at Nvidia? Unknown. “Some executives said they had never encountered Spencer Huang in the course of business,” The Wall Street Journal wrote.
"As a person who loves mess, I think the Branch Nvidians should keep this shit coming"

Employing the CEO’s relatives was already a governance risk. If the outside agitation continues to reinstate Jensen Huang, there are three key lambs that Nvidia can slaughter, and all of them are his relatives. I suppose the thing I find most astonishing is that Huang doesn’t see the writing on the wall; he has posted that if “the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” The post was met with, among other things, Altman posting a green heart in response.

Now, as a person who loves mess, I think the Branch Nvidians should keep this shit coming. I mean, Huang can nominate two people to the board of directors before the company’s shareholder meeting next year. Let’s have a stupid proxy fight and see what else leaks about Huang’s leadership and children! Of course, that will be difficult for Kress to manage — but that’s I guess what she’s getting paid for.

Up until now, Kress had been trying to rein in Huang’s spending on the AI ecosystem — financing, investments, and so on — in a huge swath of companies, according to stories in The Information and The Wall Street Journal. According to the Journal’s story, Huang noted that the vaunted deals he’d made with suppliers “were coming at him like an ‘avalanche,’” while “major cloud providers were running away from Nvidia.” This does explain Nvidia’s role as the sugar daddy for the neocloud industry. Kress reportedly pushed back on some of its agreements, apparently significantly downsizing a financial commitment to OpenAI among other things. Now, while she’ll be spending plenty of her time managing the fallout from Huang’s departure, she won’t be directly fighting with him over Nvidia’s finances.
"It publicly tells us there are limitations on what Nvidia is willing to support"

On the earnings call, analyst Stacy Rasgon of Bernstein Research asked about a new paragraph he’d noticed in the earnings release about neoclouds. Nvidia had been supplying guarantees to some neoclouds by saying it would purchase compute if no one else would. The new paragraph reads, in part, “Our commitments take effect only if the neoclouds secure financing to purchase the data center infrastructure products and the related compute capacity is deployed, made operational, and accepted by us.” Kress clarified that this meant that if neoclouds’ buildout was delayed — or they otherwise had a challenge in building the warehouse to stick the chips in — Nvidia’s guarantee “doesn’t exist anymore,” she said. “Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said.

I have no way of knowing if this language had been ready to go in the press release before Huang resigned, but it does seem notable all the same. It publicly tells us there are limitations on what Nvidia is willing to support. And knowing Kress wanted Huang to spend less on this stuff, I think it tees us up for an interesting period. Passing under the radar last week were some indications that the Federal Reserve may be about to do an interest rate hike, which is trouble for a number of companies, such as CoreWeave, that rely on debt for their data center buildouts. If we are entering a period where financing is more expensive or more difficult to get, we may see some neoclouds falter. The new paragraph in the earnings release suggests that Nvidia wants us all to know that it’s not going to bail them out forever. Bring Huang back if you want, I guess, but even he can’t control the Fed — or the increasingly odd outlook for data center financing. In the coming months, Nvidia may be better off with a woman who wants to keep the costs down.
You know who is getting money under Kress, though? Nvidia staff. They can expect raises and equity in December.

I suppose the thing I find most astonishing is that Huang doesn’t see the writing on the wall; he has posted that if “the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” The post was met with, among other things, Altman posting a green heart in response.

Now, as a person who loves mess, I think the Branch Nvidians should keep this shit coming. I mean, Huang can nominate two people to the board of directors before the company’s shareholder meeting next year. Let’s have a stupid proxy fight and see what else leaks about Huang’s leadership and children! Of course, that will be difficult for Kress to manage — but that’s I guess what she’s getting paid for.

Up until now, Kress had been trying to rein in Huang’s spending on the AI ecosystem — financing, investments, and so on — in a huge swath of companies, according to stories in The Information and The Wall Street Journal. According to the Journal’s story, Huang noted that the vaunted deals he’d made with suppliers “were coming at him like an ‘avalanche,’” while “major cloud providers were running away from Nvidia.” This does explain Nvidia’s role as the sugar daddy for the neocloud industry. Kress reportedly pushed back on some of its agreements, apparently significantly downsizing a financial commitment to OpenAI among other things. Now, while she’ll be spending plenty of her time managing the fallout from Huang’s departure, she won’t be directly fighting with him over Nvidia’s finances.

"It publicly tells us there are limitations on what Nvidia is willing to support"

Nvidia had been supplying guarantees to some neoclouds by saying it would purchase compute if no one else would. The new paragraph reads, in part, “Our commitments take effect only if the neoclouds secure financing to purchase the data center infrastructure products and the related compute capacity is deployed, made operational, and accepted by us.” Kress clarified that this meant that if neoclouds’ buildout was delayed — or they otherwise had a challenge in building the warehouse to stick the chips in — Nvidia’s guarantee “doesn’t exist anymore,” she said. “Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said.

I have no way of knowing if this language had been ready to go in the press release before Huang resigned, but it does seem notable all the same. It publicly tells us there are limitations on what Nvidia is willing to support. And knowing Kress wanted Huang to spend less on this stuff, I think it tees us up for an interesting period. Passing under the radar last week were some indications that the Federal Reserve may be about to do an interest rate hike, which is trouble for a number of companies, such as CoreWeave, that rely on debt for their data center buildouts. If we are entering a period where financing is more expensive or more difficult to get, we may see some neoclouds falter. If the glorious AI revolution rests entirely on the well-being of one man, AI is perhaps not as robust a technology as I had previously been led to believe. Nonetheless, chunks of Silicon Valley are now insisting he is indispensable. For instance, if Elon Musk is telling the truth, then Jensen Huang (the former CEO of Nvidia, a company with a market cap of about $3 trillion) has been making deals that were “a handshake with Jensen” with suppliers — “not a written contract,” Musk wrote.

Fascinating stuff to tell shareholders. But after listening to Nvidia’s first earnings call with its new CEO, Colette Kress, I do think something may have shifted. In her former role as CFO, Kress generally told Huang to stop spending so much money on financing its customers, because telling the CEO to stop spending so much goddamn money is the CFO’s job. Apparently he belittled her about this, but that’s the CEO–CFO relationship, baby! Anyway she’s the boss now, at least temporarily. I think it’s reasonable to assume that though Nvidia has for years been the AI industry’s sugar daddy, without Huang and his handshakes in the picture, it may be less liberal with its cash.

"Kress shot down the idea that Huang’s departure would lead to a brain drain within Nvidia"

Kress’ job was never going to be easy. Even without tantrums from the likes of Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Musk, both of whom seem to have a lot of free time for guys who are ostensibly running multibillion-dollar companies, having to steer a company after an event on the scale of Huang’s meltdown is a miserable task. But this woman also is now having to deal with a bunch of guys publicly insisting that Huang was the only reason Nvidia succeeded. It amused me on the call that she did the thing I often do when men decide they can bully me, which is to tap in another man who is theoretically or actually in charge of me — and so on the call, Nvidia board Chair Harvey C. Jones politely told these losers to get bent. The board does not intend to reinstate Huang, and the company won’t be taking questions about him.

On the call, Kress pointedly noted that Nvidia’s agreements with suppliers last through the end of the decade, so I suppose we must entertain the possibility that when it comes to the handshake deals, Musk is, once again, lying. This is an important thing, though — as SemiAnalysis noted in its bizarrely conspiratorial post on the situation, Nvidia is successful because it has choked off the supply chain.

Kress also shot down the idea that Huang’s departure would lead to a brain drain within Nvidia, or the kind of open internal revolt that got Sam Altman reinstated at OpenAI during “the blip” in 2023. She told investors that “our employees, we believe, are committed. They are committed to doing their life’s work at Nvidia.” Nvidia’s employees have “been working seamlessly on what they need to complete,” she added. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual.” I’m sure we’ll hear more about this in the coming days, but unlike with Altman, Huang resigned, and we all know why. And while some employees support reinstating Huang, I notice that there’s a real dearth of “we’ll quit with him” in those sentiments.

I don’t think this is going to shut the Branch Nvidians up, but I do think the board doesn’t have another choice here. Hilariously, we learned this weekend that Nvidia did not buy complete directors’ and officers’ insurance. While the individual executives’ and board members’ personal assets are shielded from lawsuits that stem from its executives’ behavior, the company is not. So if someone, or perhaps several someones, were to file a suit because of, say, Huang’s personal life and its damaging effects on the stock price, Nvidia itself is on the hook.

"The scandal isn’t mainly about the affairs, as much fun as we all have been having with them"

This is to say nothing of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s investigation — which, given how cliqued up Huang was with President Donald Trump, may be investigating on his behalf rather than investigating him — or the California attorney general going on Bloomberg TV to say that he was going to start kicking the tires on an investigation, or Huang and general counsel Tim Teter’s upcoming congressional testimony. The three actual lawyers left at the Department of Justice may be doing their own investigation, too. Elizabeth Warren seems mad. Marco Rubio’s name has been publicly attached in stories on the leaks, which makes me a little suspicious about who’s been doing the leaking.

A reminder: The scandal isn’t mainly about the affairs, as much fun as we all have been having with them. It is about Nvidia customers allegedly circumventing a ban on selling chips to China. The scandal is already big enough that US policy has been altered; the Department of Commerce informed us all on November 16th that there were new restrictions on selling chips to countries such as Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. Also, data centers around the world need licenses from the US to lease compute to companies headquartered in China.

“No one could tell them ‘no’ or put them in their place.”

You may be wondering how these restrictions will affect Nvidia’s sales. The company also addressed this, though somewhat obliquely: It raised its forecast, saying that revenue will grow by 75 percent next year. Still, given that Singapore alone was responsible for $104 billion of revenue in 2025, I am curious about the number; at the time, it was the second-biggest geographic area by revenue, dwarfed only by the US. I can’t tell you how much Singaporean sales matter to Nvidia now, because around the time that Singaporean sales reportedly started to represent half the company’s revenue, Nvidia switched its reporting methodology. https://www.theverge.com/tech/1036729/di.title: Disney’s new Star Wars animatronics interact with guests using AI
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1036729/di.author: Andrew Liszewski
paragraphs: As advanced and lifelike as the animatronic characters at Disney parks have become, they typically either stick to predefined movements and routines, or there’s an out of sight puppeteer helping make their behavior appear more spontaneous. That could soon change as Walt Disney Imagineering R&D has revealed three new Audio-Animatronic prototypes that rely on Amazon’s AWS cloud and AI capabilities to respond in unique ways to guest interactions in real-time.

The three animatronics, named Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a, and Jibu Bre’a, are based on the Star Wars alien characters called the Anzellans that were featured in The Mandalorian and Grogu film released earlier this year. The tiny bots will make their first public appearance in Las Vegas later this month where attendees of the AWS re:Invent conference will have a chance to interact with them, although the characters, and the technology powering them, could eventually find its way into Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge and other attractions at Disney’s parks.

Unlike Disney’s Olaf robot that recently debuted, there’s no one secretly using a Steam Deck gaming handheld to bring the Anzellans to life. The animatronics instead each have hidden cameras and microphones they use to capture guest movements and verbal interactions which are processed by multiple AI models running on AWS cloud servers. One “fast-decision model” generates quick responses such as the animatronics quickly making eye contact so it appears as if they’re paying attention, while larger models plan out longer interactions.

However, the Anzellans movements and verbal responses aren’t generated on the fly by AI. Every movement and line of dialogue that’s selected and triggered by the models is prewritten by Disney Imagineers to ensure the animations stay true to each character, including unique personality quirks for each one. Although AI helps guide their actions, the Anzellans never deviate from the script.

https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.author: Rani Molla
paragraphs: This summer, OpenAI paused its largest planned frontier training run after its AI agents accidentally hacked Hugging Face and early evidence suggested that its next model could independently find and exploit security flaws. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing advances in the most powerful AI models, warning that they could be used to launch cyberattacks or become harder for their own creators to control.

It was a strange moment for the AI boom. The people building the most powerful models were warning about what those models might be capable of, and investors were suddenly wondering what would happen to chip demand if the labs eased up on new models. US chip stocks bore the brunt of the sell-off.
“Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend.”

Despite the hubbub it created, whatever slowdown there was appears to have been short-lived. OpenAI had announced only a two-week pause; it restarted the run 10 days later, at the end of August, though it continued to “temporarily hold back some smaller experimental training runs.” Anthropic released upgraded versions of its Fable and Mythos frontier models in November, touting improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision.
And the companies selling the chips powering those advances are doing better than ever.

Nvidia on Tuesday posted a blockbuster quarter, with data center revenue rising 110 percent from a year ago to $107.6 billion in the three months ended October 25. The chip designer began shipping its most advanced AI computing system, the Vera Rubin NVL72, calling it the “fastest product ramp in the company’s history.” The Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments alone. The racks are already running at CoreWeave, Google, Microsoft, and Oracle. Meta plans to expand Vera Rubin deployments to train and run AI models and agents.

Nvidia name-dropped Anthropic and OpenAI, too. Anthropic has expanded access to Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers and continues to work with Nvidia on future chip designs tailored to its workloads. OpenAI is among the companies adopting Nvidia’s new Vera CPUs.

“Proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic continue to advance the frontier,” Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said on the earnings call. She said the company expects major frontier labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its data center revenue this fiscal year. Nvidia also raised its revenue growth forecast for next fiscal year from 70 percent to 75 percent.

Chipmaker AMD, meanwhile, reported its biggest quarter ever earlier this month, with revenue up 45 percent to $13.4 billion. Data center sales drove that growth, nearly doubling to $8.5 billion. OpenAI and Anthropic were among the first customers running workloads on AMD’s new high-end Helios systems, which use its latest MI450 GPUs.
Broadcom, which helps many of the biggest AI companies design their own custom chips, has yet to report earnings. But so far, there’s little sign of a frontier slowdown hurting chip sales.

Of course, even if AI labs were to significantly scale back their training ambitions, it would take a while to show up in chipmakers’ earnings. Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, told The Verge in September that it would take about six months to see the financial effects of a slowdown, owing to existing computing and memory procurement agreements. The impact could show up sooner in orders placed with chip manufacturers like TSMC.
So far, there’s little evidence of that, either: TSMC’s latest sales figures also show continued strength.
But there’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have.

“While one might argue the need for top-end GPUs will reduce with this shift toward inferencing, these workloads will collectively require more compute infrastructure than training,” Shah said. “Overall, it means a net increase in demand for all types of accelerators.”
"There’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have."

According to our analysis of the latest data from corporate spending platform Ramp, frontier model families accounted for about 60 percent of token usage among businesses using Ramp in early November — a record high and about three times their share at the start of the year. That includes OpenAI’s Astra and Sol models and Anthropic’s Opus and Fable models.
But even as businesses use more AI, their spending is only growing modestly.
“It’s not really a demand issue though,” Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp, tells The Verge. “By all measures, companies are using more AI.”
Rather, competition among AI model providers is driving down token prices so rapidly that it’s calling OpenAI and Anthropic’s revenue projections into question, Kharazian says.

That could prove beneficial for the companies supplying computing power. On Nvidia’s earnings call, Kress said token prices had fallen nearly 60 percent since May, spurring more usage. Meanwhile, rental prices for Nvidia GPUs across generations have gone up.
Nvidia and AMD are positioning their most powerful chips for both training and inference, including the demanding workloads created by AI agents.

That doesn’t necessarily mean Nvidia will maintain its dominance. As AI companies get more serious about the economics of serving their models to millions of people, they’re increasingly turning to custom chips that can do so more cheaply than general-purpose GPUs. Counterpoint expects shipments of custom AI server processors to surpass those of data center GPUs by 2028.
“Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend,” Shah said.

Indeed, on Nvidia’s earnings call, UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked Kress whether the company would be willing to sacrifice some of its hefty profit margins as frontier labs increasingly invest in custom chips and prioritize computing efficiency. Kress maintained that Nvidia’s systems justify their pricing and reiterated the company’s gross margin outlook.
For companies like Nvidia, the bigger threat may not be that AI companies slow down, but that they find cheaper chips on which to keep going.
