https://www.theverge.com/games/1036140/w.title: Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories
https://www.theverge.com/games/1036140/w.author: Jay Peters
paragraphs: Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims, is working on a new game — and it’s built around AI. The new title, focused on your memories, is called MyMems. Like Wright’s other titles, it sounds extremely ambitious, giving players a new way to explore worlds they create on their own. “We want to take your autobiography and turn it into a toy world,” he tells The Verge.

The MyMems website describes the mobile game as a “social simulation” with worlds “built from your memories and the people who shaped you.” You can add “memories” to your game, like speaking a short story to your phone, and those memories are generated into pieces you can place on the game’s map. Your worlds can also include AI-powered avatars, which can represent people you know in your life. Ideally, as you play, the planet starts to become a “map of your psyche,” kind of like Inside Out, Wright says. Worlds can be private, but you can also share them with others.
Here’s another way to think of it, from Virginia McArthur, executive producer and GM at MyMems developer Gallium Studios: “It’s a cozy world builder with a really deep social simulation underneath.”

I’ll admit that I don’t totally get it, and it seems like a tricky idea to grasp without playing it. Still, as heady of a concept as it might be — turning your memories into a game world — Wright and team still want it to be fun. “This isn’t meant to be your legacy diary necessarily,” says Anthony Maitz, a product manager at Gallium Studios. “It’s meant to just be something you kind of play around with.” However, Maitz notes that what you’re working toward is a “proxy” of you — a word that seems to be the inspiration of the game’s earlier title, Proxi: Yesterday’s You Tomorrow. The game will use the “Behavior Engine” from a company called Artificial Agency, which makes AI tech for video games, as a “foundational technology.”

Like other industries, gaming is starting to reckon with generative AI. Early AI virtual worlds created with models from a startup backed by a Pixar cofounder and Google’s Project Genie weren’t experiences you’d actually want to spend dedicated time with, and indie developers I spoke to in March were largely opposed to the technology. But AI technology has taken some big leaps this year with companies like Google, Meta, and Roblox now letting users make games with AI right from their phone, and retro gaming becoming overrun with AI-powered ports of classic titles.

Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said earlier this year that generative AI has “zero part in what Rockstar Games is building” with GTA VI. But even as a recent industry survey indicated that more game developers are starting to use generative AI as part of their job, workers are pushing back against generative AI use, and the technology is at the center of fierce debates over indie game awards.

Many players are rejecting AI outright, and I wondered if the Gallium Studios team was worried about opposition toward MyMems’ use of AI. Wright says he has three boys at home and that they are all “pretty negative” on AI. He attributes negativity over AI to be toward the meaning of art and authorship and credit, a concern he calls “well-founded.” But he also calls AI an “amazing tool.”

“We’re not making slop,” says McArthur. But Maitz notes that while the team has “been concerned” about a negative response to the generative AI use, they’ve learned that people don’t mind when they use AI in a “Scribblenauts-y style” for things like having the game make a high school. The team also found that people got “addicted” to a test app with a character creator, including Maitz’s own daughter, who he says “hates” AI. “By making it so that the player is authoring it over and over, bit by bit, it doesn’t really feel like you cheated,” Maitz says.
“We’re not making slop.”

MyMems, which is set to launch in 2027, will join a growing field of other social simulations, like Krafton’s Inzoi and Nintendo’s smash hit Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. But none quite have the pull of The Sims, which remains one of EA’s most important franchises. With The Sims, Wright says that many people tried making their real families in the game.

“It was interesting how people really were naturally trying to map this game, which was like a little toy, onto their real life,” he says. With MyMems, that’s what the team is trying to do the “follow-through” on — what if they made the whole game focused on you?

Imagine opening a family scrapbook and the way people and things jump out, Wright explains. “As you go through more and more pages, pretty soon you have this whole little circus of people and events and things from your life.” It’s chaos, he says. “I want something that feels kind of like that.”
Update, November 18th: Added context about Artificial Agency.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1036445/nv.title: Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1036445/nv.author: Jess Weatherbed
paragraphs: Nvidia has stopped sending its advanced AI chips to China despite the approval it received from the White House to do so in December last year. The announcement was made by interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress during an earnings call on Tuesday, marking a notable shift for the company that, under former CEO Jensen Huang, fought for the right to ship its powerful Hopper architecture H200 chips to China.

“Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licenced Hopper data center products to China,” Kress said. She did not explain why Nvidia was ceasing its H200 processor shipments or clarify whether Nvidia would pursue other business with China in the future.

The pivot comes after Huang stepped down from his position as Nvidia CEO last week following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, one with a woman who was suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia already faced difficulties around offloading the AI chips prior to this scandal, however. Concerns were raised about failings to properly vet Chinese companies that were approved to handle the H200 AI chips. Reuters also reported earlier this month that around 600,000 H200 chips were stuck in Hong Kong after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports, with China seeking to reduce its dependency on US technology.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1036796/go.title: Google is forcing Android app developers to properly support foldables
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1036796/go.author: Jay Peters
paragraphs: Now that Apple’s foldable is here, Google wants to make sure apps on Android foldables are a good experience. Starting in April 2027, Google is going to require Android developers to make sure their apps have a baseline level of support for foldables. If they don’t, developers risk not being able to publish or update their apps or have reduced visibility for their apps on Google Play.

Google says Android apps must meet its “Tier 3 — Adaptive ready” standard. “Apps must fill the available display area without letterboxing or compatibility modes,” Google says. “Apps must preserve state (scroll position, text input, media playback) during rotation, folding/unfolding, and resizing, while supporting multi-window environments.” (The other two tiers are “Adaptive optimized” and “Adaptive differentiated” and take further advantage of the possibilities of foldables.) As of the April 2027 deadline, developers also will have to include three foldable screenshots for their app listings. Developers can start publishing their foldable screenshots today.

Similar requirements will apply to games, though developers have until August 2027 to get their titles ready for Android foldables, Google says. (Google “plans to extend” its requirements to other large-screen devices like tablets and Googlebook laptops in “future phases.”) However, game developers will still need to share three foldable screenshots for app listings starting in April.

The changes are being announced just weeks after Apple launched the iPhone Duo, which already has more than 200,000 optimized apps, though some developers are still figuring out Apple’s foldable form factor.

https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.title: Canva adds an AI ‘off’ button
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.author: Emma Roth
paragraphs: Canva will now allow you to turn off its generative AI features. With this change, you can disable the graphic design platform’s array of AI tools, such as its AI photo-extending Magic Expand feature, as well as turn off the ability to generate images with its Canva chatbot.

This toggle doesn’t turn off every AI-powered feature on Canva, however. That includes Canva’s background remover and its Magic Grab tool, which lets you select an object in an image and move it somewhere else. “Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design,” Canva says.
The toggle still turns off many of Canva’s other AI features, including Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code, AI Shapes, and more.

Since Canva’s big push into AI in 2023, some users have expressed frustration with the influx of AI features and asked for ways to turn them off. Canva has only continued to expand on its AI-powered image-editing suite since then, by rolling out a prompt-powered editing update in April and launching its first in-house AI model, Canva Craft, last month.

You can also now switch a toggle to see less AI content in Canva’s content library. Switching this option on means you’ll see human-created content first when searching through Canva’s library for templates, graphics, and other design elements. Canva says a “small portion” of its library consists of AI-generated content, and that any design that uses one of these elements will have an AI label in its metadata.

To turn off Canva’s AI features, head to Profile > Settings > Permission, and then toggle off Enable generative AI features. You can choose to see less AI-generated content by going to Profile > Your account > AI personalization, and then turning on the option to show less AI content. These switches are available to both free and paid users.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1037100/ap.title: I let Apple’s always-listening AI summarize my life for two weeks
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1037100/ap.author: Victoria Song
paragraphs: I’ve been asking myself this quite a bit over the last month or so while testing both the Amazon Bee Frontier and Siri Recap on the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Both enable a wearable to ambiently listen to your conversations and, using AI, summarize them for you. Why? So you can remember better and, hopefully, stay more present.

The main difference is that Amazon’s Bee takes a maximalist (and frankly reality-bending) approach, whereas Apple is going for a more minimalist, privacy-first take. Both, however, require explicit disclosures to the people around you about recording what they say, and potentially follow-up explanations about how exactly this all works. This past week, I’ve been testing the Siri Recap beta to see if Apple’s is a less dystopian experience.

Apple presents Siri Recap as a sort of backup notetaker. As a college student, perhaps you’re less concerned about writing down what a professor says and can just take in the lecture. Say you attend a parent-teacher conference solo. You can focus on the discussion and then whip out your phone later to reference what was said when explaining it to your spouse.

These are fairly innocuous scenarios. But given the discourse around privacy and surveillance gadgets this year, it’s easy to imagine how always-listening devices could be misused. Apple has taken great care to create a version of this that at least considers that bystanders may feel uncomfortable knowing someone else’s Apple Watch may be taking notes on what they say.

The feature isn’t turned on by default — you have to opt in. Users can then program when the feature turns on. For example, only at the office between the hours of 1 to 2PM on weekdays. Unless saved, all recaps are also set to self-destruct after your choice of one, three, or seven days. Within the summaries, there’s no viewable transcript detailing who said what and when. That makes these recaps more difficult to use as “receipts” for arguments, court cases, or blackmail. There’s also no raw audio file that’s ever saved. Not to get too into the weeds, but the audio gets processed and then immediately deleted through a secure exclave within the 2026 Apple Watch’s S11 chip that’s inaccessible to Apple and other third parties. The vast majority of the processing is also done locally. Whatever does get sent to the cloud is done through Apple’s Private Cloud Compute. Because the feature requires this hardware, it’s impossible to use on older Apple Watches.

It’s not perfect. Unlike Live Rewind, another audio intelligence feature, there’s no outward indicator or audio chime to signal recording intent. So, if you do decide to ethically disclose your usage, you have to be prepared to explain everything I just described if someone asks questions.
Maybe that’s worth it — if Siri can be trusted to be truly helpful.

The reality is that better privacy often means a less useful AI product. The more AI knows about you, the better the summaries from these devices tend to be. To preserve privacy, Apple prevents Siri from learning everything about you and the people in your life. For example, Siri Recap doesn’t train on your voice. Excellent for privacy! But that also means Siri has a much harder time discerning when you’re actually having a conversation. That leads to some funny but ultimately unhelpful recaps.

For instance, I was watching a TikTok in which a chronically ill creator was updating their followers about being sent to the emergency room because of sepsis. Siri recapped that video as if I, or potentially someone I knew, had been sent to the ER. Another TikTok weighing in on an AITA Reddit thread got summarized as if I had discussed a shady homewrecker named Dana trying to seduce her bestie’s husband by wearing a glittery blue bikini top at a concert. Because attribution was stripped, the summary could read as if I were the guilty spouse returning between 2 and 3AM, covered in Dana’s glitter. In both instances, the lack of attribution also made the resulting summaries hilarious and confusing.

Also, neither video was something I wanted or needed to remember. I suspect Siri summarized them because I was playing the audio out loud on my phone, which sits pretty close to my Apple Watch. There’s an easy workaround here. Siri Recap automatically turns off if you use headphones, meaning I could just eliminate recaps from podcasts, audiobooks, TV shows, etc., by always wearing my AirPods. But that’s me adjusting my behavior to accommodate Siri’s inability to discern when I’m talking.
Another quirk: Siri doesn’t know what I want to remember or find memorable from a given conversation.

I turned on Siri Recap during my briefing and demos for the new smart glasses from Google, Samsung, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker. When I sat down to write, the resulting recap helped me remember the main topics discussed. I also found it useful that a handful of interview recaps were linked to a corresponding Voice Memos file. The thing is, Siri Recap heavily prioritizes restating the facts. That means bullet points tend to emphasize statistics, factoids, and dates. That’s useful in straightforward planning meetings, but less useful for what you might personally find to be a salient takeaway. For example, in an interview with a source, what I found most interesting was a personal anecdote and some strong opinions about RFK Jr. My Siri Recap from that interview omitted it in favor of more concrete details.

Meanwhile, personal conversations are rarely as straightforward. Work meetings often have agendas. Chats with friends and family can jump across a zillion topics in the span of 10 minutes. Plus, most of my conversations should be deleted from my brain to make room for the really important things. I didn’t need to see a detailed summary of what my spouse and I thought of the last episode of Nathan Fielder’s The Curse. (It was bonkers.) I’d love to never revisit a 20-minute argument with my cousin over hardwired versus battery-powered smoke detectors. (Too bad, the recap outlined the main points.) A recap of my spouse and me debating movie recommendations might be a useful recap, but it just says “seeking less anxiety-inducing media” and “refusing to ever watch Star Wars.”

My recaps were also a lesson in why conversational context matters. Sometimes, Siri correctly assumes that gossip is irrelevant to the broader conversation at hand and omits it entirely. Other times, its blunt, matter-of-fact recaps of jokes or my friends venting read like an unhinged Regina George from Mean Girls building an AI-generated Burn Book.
That inconsistency is why relying on AI to make judgment calls on your behalf feels unsettling.

I keep getting stuck on what problem these features are meant to solve. Tech companies usually say ambient listening is meant to help jog our memories or to help us stay more present. Which brings me back to my initial question: Was it worth it? Did Apple’s efforts to protect privacy prove we can have our AI note-taking cake and eat it too?

Outside a few work-related scenarios, I haven’t found Siri Recaps to be useful. Even writing this, I spent a lot of time scrolling to find a small handful of examples that I would want to discuss. On the plus side, I’m not terribly worried about people snooping through my recaps. Of the more than 50 recaps generated, I’m confident 90 percent would be gibberish for anyone but me.

Conversely, I found more of what Amazon’s Bee generated to be “useful.” But after seeing Bee’s raw transcripts and summaries of every spoken moment in my life, I believe we’re not meant to live that way. I’ve since nuked all my Bee data.

But even if I prefer Apple’s approach for privacy reasons, my gut says this tech isn’t the answer for jogging memories or staying present. Whenever I’ve forgotten things, the negative consequences have rarely — if ever — led to irrevocably changing my life for the worse. Usually, it’s a bitter lesson that’s forced me to grow and adapt. And anytime I’m not present in the moment, it’s usually because I’m on my phone.

Ambient listening wearables can be helpful when used in low-stakes, straightforward situations where everyone consents. But for me, it’s often in little ways that have many less-invasive alternatives. I mean having to explain to the less tech-savvy people in my life that my Apple Watch now has this feature that recaps our conversations. Having to watch how their faces mull it over. Having to muster the will to answer their questions about how Apple handles privacy with this feature versus other devices I’ve tested. Having to smile when my spouse jokes about censoring their humor because of my job. Having to write in my work Slack that when my coworkers see me in the office, I am testing AI devices that may be recording any conversation, and that I am happy to turn them off if it makes them uncomfortable. Having to weigh whether I have enough bandwidth or time before every conversation with strangers to be thoughtful and ethical.
Right now, there are no established cultural norms telling me how to easily pay this cost. All I know is that if I turn the feature off, I don’t have to think about it at all.

Whenever I’ve forgotten things, the negative consequences have rarely — if ever — led to irrevocably changing my life for the worse. Usually, it’s a bitter lesson that’s forced me to grow and adapt. And anytime I’m not present in the moment, it’s usually because I’m on my phone.

Ambient listening wearables can be helpful when used in low-stakes, straightforward situations where everyone consents. But for me, it’s often in little ways that have many less-invasive alternatives. I mean having to explain to the less tech-savvy people in my life that my Apple Watch now has this feature that recaps our conversations. Having to watch how their faces mull it over. Having to muster the will to answer their questions about how Apple handles privacy with this feature versus other devices I’ve tested. Having to smile when my spouse jokes about censoring their humor because of my job. Having to write in my work Slack that when my coworkers see me in the office, I am testing AI devices that may be recording any conversation, and that I am happy to turn them off if it makes them uncomfortable. Having to weigh whether I have enough bandwidth or time before every conversation with strangers to be thoughtful and ethical.

Right now, there are no established cultural norms telling me how to easily pay this cost. All I know is that if I turn the feature off, I don’t have to think about it at all.
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1037100/ap.lead_paragraph: I’ve been asking myself this quite a bit over the last month or so while testing both the Amazon Bee Frontier and Siri Recap on the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Both enable a wearable to ambiently listen to your conversations and, using AI, summarize them for you. Why? So you can remember better and, hopefully, stay more present.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1037535/go.title: Blue Origin will launch Google’s AI server satellites in 2029
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1037535/go.author: Emma Roth
paragraphs: Google is teaming up with Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to launch its AI server satellites. The companies announced on Thursday that Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket will shuttle satellites equipped with Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) into space in the first quarter of 2029.

The partnership is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, a moonshot plan that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google deployed its first AI server satellite in October, successfully booting up its TPUs and using the on-board Gemma 4 model to transmit an AI-generated haiku to Earth.

The Blue Origin launch will be the “first dedicated heavy lift launch” for Project Suncatcher, putting satellites with the “computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack” into sun-synchronous orbit. Google’s AI server satellite previously launched aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket as part of a “rideshare” launch that included several other payloads.
